cc: Unable to urinate with lower abdominal pressure

HPI: 26 yo f. Patient reports: I last passed urine normally 10 hours ago. The pressure is low in the center of my abdomen. There is no flank radiation. It is a tight, painful fullness. model_note.O:
Vitals: T 98.6 F oral, P 94 bpm, BP 148/86 mmHg, R 18 rpm, Pulse Ox 98% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert and distressed by lower abdominal pressure.

Heart: Regular rhythm without murmur.

Lungs: Clear breath sounds bilaterally.

Abd: Visible lower midline abdominal fullness. Bowel sounds present. Tender rounded fullness in the suprapubic region. Dull percussion over the suprapubic fullness.

Neuro: Lower extremity strength 5/5 bilaterally.

Osteopathic: T10 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
A: 2. Pelvic mass causing bladder outlet obstruction
3. Neurogenic bladder due to multiple sclerosis
P: 1. Arrange immediate emergency or urology assessment for bladder decompression; obtain bladder volume, renal function, urinalysis and pregnancy testing without delaying treatment; stop further diphenhydramine pending clinician review; explain retention and arrange supervised disposition today with a catheter/reassessment plan before discharge.

2. After acute decompression, assess menstrual/pelvic history and obtain pelvic imaging if obstruction persists or a mass is suspected; arrange urology or gynecology referral as indicated; explain that a possible mass is not a confirmed cancer diagnosis.

3. Ask about prior episodic visual, sensory or motor symptoms and examine relevant neurologic function; arrange neurology evaluation and targeted imaging only when supported; explain that urinary retention alone does not establish multiple sclerosis and must not delay immediate bladder care.

model_note.S:
cc: Unable to urinate with lower abdominal pressure

HPI: 26 yo f. Patient reports: I last passed urine normally 6 hours ago. The pressure is low in the center of my abdomen. There is no flank radiation. It is a tight, painful fullness. The pressure is 8/10. It has become worse through the day. I started an over-the-counter cold medicine yesterday. Trying again does not relieve it. The fullness keeps increasing. I have tried to urinate several times without success. For months I have had a weak stream but never complete blockage. I cannot pass urine despite a strong urge. My stream has been slow to start for months.

Patient perspective: Will a catheter hurt?

PMH: Episodes of difficulty relaxing to urinate for 2 years, never previously assessed; no neurologic disease.

PSH: No pelvic surgery or catheterization history.

Meds: No daily prescription medicine; took diphenhydramine 25 mg last night for cold symptoms.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

SH: Never smoked tobacco. One alcoholic drink weekly. No recreational drugs. Engineering technician; lives with husband.

FH: Father had prostate enlargement; mother had hypertension; brother healthy.

ROS: Urinary - Reports retention. Reports hesitancy. Denies hematuria. Neurologic - Denies back pain. Denies saddle numbness. Denies leg weakness. General - Denies fever. Denies chills. Denies fatigue.
Reproductive history: I do not think I am pregnant, but I have not taken a pregnancy test.
Reproductive history: My last period was 2 weeks ago.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 98.6 F oral, P 94 bpm, BP 148/86 mmHg, R 18 rpm, Pulse Ox 98% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert and distressed by lower abdominal pressure.

Heart: Regular rhythm without murmur.

Lungs: Clear breath sounds bilaterally.

Abd: Visible lower midline abdominal fullness. Bowel sounds present. Tender rounded fullness in the suprapubic region. Dull percussion over the suprapubic fullness.

Neuro: Lower extremity strength 5/5 bilaterally.

Osteopathic: T10 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
A: 2. Pelvic mass causing bladder outlet obstruction
3. Neurogenic bladder due to multiple sclerosis
P: 1. Arrange immediate emergency or urology assessment for bladder decompression; obtain bladder volume, renal function, urinalysis and pregnancy testing without delaying treatment; stop further diphenhydramine pending clinician review; explain retention and arrange supervised disposition today with a catheter/reassessment plan before discharge.

2. After acute decompression, assess menstrual/pelvic history and obtain pelvic imaging if obstruction persists or a mass is suspected; arrange urology or gynecology referral as indicated; explain that a possible mass is not a confirmed cancer diagnosis.

3. Ask about prior episodic visual, sensory or motor symptoms and examine relevant neurologic function; arrange neurology evaluation and targeted imaging only when supported; explain that urinary retention alone does not establish multiple sclerosis and must not delay immediate bladder care.

A: 2. Pelvic mass causing bladder outlet obstruction
3. Neurogenic bladder due to multiple sclerosis
P: 1. Arrange immediate emergency or urology assessment for bladder decompression; obtain bladder volume, renal function, urinalysis and pregnancy testing without delaying treatment; stop further diphenhydramine pending clinician review; explain retention and arrange supervised disposition today with a catheter/reassessment plan before discharge. Ask whom she wants involved, preserve privacy and explain catheter comfort and care in practical terms.

2. After acute decompression, assess menstrual/pelvic history and obtain pelvic imaging if obstruction persists or a mass is suspected; arrange urology or gynecology referral as indicated; explain that a possible mass is not a confirmed cancer diagnosis.

3. Ask about prior episodic visual, sensory or motor symptoms and examine relevant neurologic function; arrange neurology evaluation and targeted imaging only when supported; explain that urinary retention alone does not establish multiple sclerosis and must not delay immediate bladder care.
